chunks: And Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Ukba, who said:

Sadir al-Sayrafi came to me and said: Indeed, Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) sends you greetings and says to you: 'What is wrong with you that you do not perform Hajj? Borrow and perform Hajj.' Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The meaning in these two narrations is that we should interpret them as applying to the one who has wealth that will return to him, so he can pay off his debt. As for the one who does not have that, it is not permissible for him to borrow and perform Hajj, because the Hajj that has become obligatory upon him indicates this distinction.

key_terms.ابْنُ أَبِي عُمَيْرٍ: Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, a prominent narrator of hadith
key_terms.الْحَجُّ: Hajj, the annual Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca
key_terms.سَدِيرٌ الصَّيْرَفِيُّ: Sadir al-Sayrafi, a companion of the Imams known for his role in currency exchange

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to borrow money to perform Hajj in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *al-Istibsar*, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Wajih provides a nuanced juristic distinction regarding borrowing for Hajj, ruling that it is permissible only if the borrower possesses assets to ensure repayment, thereby avoiding the burden of unpayable debt. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on financial responsibility and the preservation of one's creditworthiness as a prerequisite for fulfilling the obligatory pilgrimage.
